paragraphs: Contoso claims intake project.
Contoso engaged us for its claims intake project. Contoso is a mid sized general insurer that sells motor and home policies to customers in the UK, and its claims team handles every claim in house.
Before the project, Contoso received claims by email, telephone and a paper form, and each channel was keyed into the policy system by hand.
Handling a simple claim took 11 days on average, and the claims team spent most of its time re-entering data rather than assessing cases.
Peak weeks after storms produced a backlog of about 4,000 open claims, and customers had no way to see the status of their claim.
Regulators expected faster first responses, so Contoso set a goal of acknowledging every claim within one working day.
Photographs and repair estimates were attached to emails that were not linked to any claim record, and documents were sometimes lost.
The scope was a single claims intake service that accepts claims from the web, the mobile app and the call centre, and creates one claim record for each.
Deliverables were an intake API, an event stream that publishes every claim change, a document store linked to the claim, and a status page for customers.
The service validates each claim against the policy at the moment it is submitted and routes simple claims to automatic acceptance.
Contoso adjusters receive a single work queue that ranks claims by severity and age, replacing the three separate mailboxes used before.
The policy administration system stayed as it was and is reached only through its existing interface, so it was outside the scope.
The work was delivered in three phases over 14 months: discovery and design, a pilot with the motor claims team, and a staged rollout to all claim types.
The team had 9 engineers, a product owner from Contoso, and two claims specialists who joined the weekly reviews.
The programme ran from January 2023 to February 2024, with the pilot live in June 2023 and the last claim type moved in February 2024.
Each phase ended with a demonstration to the claims leadership, and releases were made every two weeks behind feature flags.
Old and new intake ran side by side during the pilot, so adjusters could fall back to the old mailboxes without losing a claim.
Kafka carries the claim events, with one topic for each claim type and a retention of 30 days so that downstream systems can replay them.
PostgreSQL holds the claim records, and the document store keeps attachments in encrypted object storage linked by claim number.
The intake API sits behind an API gateway that enforces OAuth 2.0 tokens and a rate limit for each channel.
The integration with the policy system uses its existing SOAP interface, wrapped in a small adapter so the rest of the platform sees plain events.
Notifications to customers are sent by email and text message when a claim is received, assigned and settled.
The intake API is described in an OpenAPI 3.0 specification that the channel teams used to build against.
Average handling time for a simple claim fell from 11 days to 4 days, a reduction of 64 percent.
More than 70 percent of motor claims are now accepted automatically, and the open claim backlog fell to about 600 after the next storm season.
Customers now receive an acknowledgement within one working day for all claims, and the status page is used in 82 percent of follow up contacts.
Running the old and new intake side by side during the pilot gave adjusters the confidence to move, and the team would do the same again.
Agreeing the event names with the claims team early saved rework, whereas the policy system adapter took longer than planned.

paragraphs: Northwind stock forecasting project.
Northwind engaged us for its stock forecasting project. Northwind Traders is a retail chain with 120 stores in Germany that sells groceries and household goods.
Store managers ordered stock from experience and a weekly spreadsheet, so popular items ran out while slow items piled up in the back rooms.
Fresh products were the hardest case, because Northwind wrote off 9 percent of its fresh stock each year as waste.
Promotions and local events were not reflected in orders, so a sale could empty a shelf by the second day.
Head office had no single view of stock across stores and warehouses, and planners reconciled figures by hand every Monday.
Northwind wanted forecasts for each store and product, refreshed every night, that store managers could trust and override.
The sponsor was the chief operating officer, who wanted a measurable saving in the first region before the other two regions committed to the new way of working.
The scope was a demand forecasting service that predicts daily sales for each product in each store for the coming 14 days.
Deliverables were a feature pipeline that prepares sales, price, weather and calendar data, a set of forecasting models, and an ordering dashboard for store managers.
The dashboard proposes an order quantity for every product and shows the reasons, such as an upcoming promotion, so managers can accept or change it.
The service also publishes forecasts to the warehouse planning tool, so replenishment follows the same numbers as store orders.
Pricing decisions, supplier contracts and the point of sale software were outside the scope of the project.
Stores were grouped by size and region for the pilot, so that the results could be compared fairly with stores that kept ordering in the old way.
The project ran in four phases over 10 months: data preparation, model development, a pilot in 12 stores, and a rollout to all stores.
The team had 7 people, made up of data engineers, data scientists, a front end developer and a delivery lead.
Work started in March 2023 and the rollout to all stores finished in December 2023, with the pilot running from July to September.
Forecast accuracy was measured against a hold out period of eight weeks before each phase gate, and store managers joined the pilot reviews.
Models were retrained every week and compared with the live model before replacing it.
Nightly sales and stock data lands in Azure storage and is transformed by Spark jobs into one table with a row for each store, product and day.
The forecasting models are written in Python and use gradient boosted trees, with a separate model for fresh products that is retrained every week.
Forecasts and order proposals are served by a REST service running on Kubernetes, and the dashboard calls it with OAuth 2.0 tokens issued for each store.
Weather data comes from a public weather service and the promotion calendar is read from the existing planning tool, both through scheduled imports.
The API follows the OpenAPI 3.0 specification, and the model results are stored in the MLflow registry together with the data used to train them.
Forecast error for fresh products fell from 31 percent to 18 percent, measured as weighted absolute error across all stores.
Fresh stock waste fell from 9 percent to 6 percent of fresh stock, and shelf availability for promoted items rose to 96 percent.
Planners stopped the Monday reconciliation, which saved about 20 hours of work each week at head office.
Store managers trusted the forecasts once the dashboard showed the reasons, and the override rate dropped steadily after the pilot.
Weather data helped less than expected, while the promotion calendar mattered a great deal, so data quality work should start with promotions.

paragraphs: Woodgrove payments gateway project.
Woodgrove engaged us for its payments gateway project. Woodgrove is a retail bank that serves consumers and small businesses in Ireland.
Woodgrove processed card and account payments through four separate systems, each with its own interface and its own release cycle.
Adding a new payment scheme took about 9 months because every system had to be changed and tested separately.
Operations staff could not see the state of a payment end to end, so a customer enquiry meant searching in up to four screens.
Nightly batch files delayed some payments to the next working day, while customers and businesses expected instant confirmation.
The old gateway ran on hardware near the end of its support life, which was a risk Woodgrove wanted to close within the year.
The programme was sponsored by the head of operations and reviewed every month by a steering group that included risk, compliance and technology leaders from the bank.
The scope was a single payments gateway that receives instructions from digital channels and routes them to the right payment scheme.
Deliverables were a common payment message model, adapters for SEPA credit transfers and card payments, a rules based router and an operations console.
Each payment is screened for sanctions and checked for duplicates before it is sent, and the result is kept with the payment.
The operations console shows every payment on one timeline, with its messages, its status and the person who last touched it.
Core account ledgers and the card processor were kept as they were, and the gateway connected to them through their existing interfaces.
The business case was reviewed by the finance and operations directors, who asked for a pilot with measured results before any wider commitment was made.
Delivery took 16 months in four phases: foundation, credit transfers, card payments and decommissioning of the old systems.
The team had 14 engineers and testers, with a Woodgrove architect and an operations lead working alongside them.
The programme started in April 2022 and the last old system was switched off in July 2023.
Every scheme was first run in shadow mode, where the new gateway processed copies of live payments and its results were compared with the old systems.
Cut over happened one scheme at a time, by moving a small share of traffic first and then the rest after two quiet weeks.
The gateway runs as containers on Kubernetes in two data centres, with Kafka carrying payment events between the services.
Payment state is stored in PostgreSQL with synchronous replication between the centres, so no accepted payment is lost if one centre fails.
Messages use the ISO 20022 standard internally, and the adapters translate to and from the formats each scheme requires.
Sanctions screening is provided by a vendor product called through an internal service, and its answer is stored with the payment record.
Connections to partners use mutual TLS, and customer facing APIs follow the OpenAPI 3.0 specification with OAuth 2.0 authorisation.
A new payment scheme can now be added in about 6 weeks instead of 9 months.
Payments are confirmed within 10 seconds at any hour, and the nightly batch delay has been removed.
Customer enquiries about a payment take 3 minutes to resolve instead of 12, because operations staff use one screen.
Shadow mode found 31 differences in rounding and timing rules before any customer was affected, which justified its cost.
Moving traffic in small shares made each cut over a routine event, and the team would keep that approach.
Requirements were gathered in ride alongs with drivers and in workshops with dispatchers in each region, and the findings were written up as a short list of design rules.

paragraphs: Tailspin route planning project.
Tailspin engaged us for its route planning project. Tailspin is a parcel delivery company with 340 vans that operate in Australia.
Drivers received a printed list each morning that dispatchers had built by hand, and the routes were rarely the shortest.
Same day changes, such as a missed delivery or a new pickup, were phoned to the driver and often forgotten.
Vans drove 18 percent more kilometres than needed, according to an internal study, and fuel was the largest cost after wages.
Customers were given a delivery window of a whole day, which led to missed deliveries and repeat visits for about 1 parcel in 8.
Dispatchers worked in three regional offices with three different tools, so spare capacity in one region could not help another.
Security and resilience requirements were agreed with the risk team at the start, so that the design could be reviewed against them at each phase gate and again before the final cut over.
The scope was a route planning service that builds the daily routes for every van from the parcels, the time windows and the vehicle limits.
Deliverables were a planning engine, a driver app with turn by turn navigation, a dispatcher console and a customer tracking page.
The planner re-optimises during the day when a parcel is added or a van is delayed, and sends the change to the driver app at once.
Customers choose a two hour delivery window and can follow the van on a map, which replaced the whole day window.
Vehicle maintenance, payroll and the existing parcel scanning devices remained outside the project.
A shared list of design rules, kept short and visible to the whole team, helped the developers and the optimisation engineers settle disagreements quickly.
The project took 11 months in three phases: a planning engine proof, a pilot in one region and a rollout to all three regions.
The team had 8 people, including two optimisation engineers, three developers, a designer, a tester and a delivery lead.
Work began in September 2022, the pilot ran from January to April 2023, and the third region went live in July 2023.
Dispatchers and drivers from the pilot region sat in the team every week and tested each release on real routes.
Each region went live on a Monday, with the old tool kept read only for two weeks as a reference.
The planning engine uses the OR-Tools solver library, wrapped in a Python service that scales out on Kubernetes when many routes are planned at once.
Road distances and travel times come from a map data service, and live traffic is added every five minutes.
The driver app is built with React and receives updates through push messages, and it keeps working offline in areas without coverage.
Parcel and vehicle data is read from the existing parcel system through a Kafka topic, and routes are written back to a PostgreSQL database.
Route geometry is exchanged as GeoJSON, the public API is described in an OpenAPI 3.0 specification, and sign in uses OAuth 2.0.
Distance driven fell by 14 percent, which cut fuel use by a similar share across the fleet.
Deliveries made at the first attempt rose from 87 percent to 95 percent.
Dispatchers needed 35 minutes to plan the morning routes for a region instead of three hours.
Drivers adopted the app quickly because they helped design it, and the pilot feedback changed the layout of the stop list twice.
Offline operation should have been designed earlier, as the first pilot builds failed in areas without coverage.
The steering group asked for the lessons to be shared with other teams in the bank, and the shadow mode approach has since been described in the internal engineering guidance.

paragraphs: Litware citizen portal project.
Litware engaged us for its citizen portal project. Litware runs public services for a regional government in Sweden and employs about 400 case officers.
The project was sponsored by the director of citizen services, who asked for a single front door to services that residents use several times a year.
Residents had to visit three separate websites and two offices to apply for permits, benefits and housing support, and each asked for the same documents again.
The three websites had grown over many years, each owned by a different department, and none of them shared accounts, forms or content with the others, so a change of address had to be repeated.
Applications arrived on paper or by email, and case officers typed them into the register, which caused errors and a median wait of 23 days.
Residents could not see where their application was, so the call centre answered about 1,200 status calls each month.
Accessibility complaints were rising, because the old websites did not work well with screen readers or on small phones.
Interviews with residents showed that people with the greatest need, such as older residents and new arrivals, were the ones who found the old websites hardest to use.
The scope was a single citizen portal where residents sign in once, submit applications online, upload documents and follow the status of each case.
Deliverables were the portal, an application form builder for the service teams, a status tracker, and a notification service built with Python and PostgreSQL.
Sign in uses OpenID Connect with the national identity provider, and the portal meets WCAG 2.1 level AA for accessibility.
The case register used by the officers stayed in place, and the portal sends each application to it through its existing import.
Services that need a signature or a meeting in person, such as some housing decisions, were kept as offline steps, and the portal books the appointment and reminds the resident.
The project took 9 months in three phases: research and design, a pilot with housing support, and the launch of permits and benefits.
The team had 6 people, including two developers, a designer, a content specialist, a tester and a delivery lead.
Work started in February 2024, the housing pilot opened in June 2024, and the full launch took place in October 2024.
Residents and case officers took part in usability sessions after every sprint, and 14 sessions were held in total.
The team also ran a small private beta with 200 residents before each launch, and the findings were reviewed by the steering group before the next service went live.
Median wait for a decision fell from 23 days to 9 days, and 71 percent of applications are now submitted online.
Status calls to the call centre fell from about 1,200 to about 300 each month.
Satisfaction with the application process, measured by a short survey after each decision, was reported to the steering group every month throughout the first year.
The steering group met every month and included the director of citizen services, a representative of the case officers and a resident who volunteered after the first usability sessions.
Usability sessions after every sprint found problems early, and the team would book them before the design starts next time.
The service teams needed more time than planned to rewrite their forms in plain language, and this work should start in the first month.
The portal is now maintained by a small in house team that Litware trained during the project, and the supplier role has moved from delivery to occasional advice.
Further services are planned for the next year, and the portal was built so that each service team can add its own forms without waiting for the developers.

paragraphs: Adventure Works booking platform project.
Adventure Works engaged us for its booking platform project. Adventure Works is a travel operator that sells guided trips and activity holidays across Spain.
Bookings were taken in three systems, one for trips, one for activities and one for accommodation, so a customer who wanted all three had to book separately.
Availability was updated by hand each evening, and about 6 percent of bookings were rejected afterwards because the place had already been sold.
Peak season traffic slowed the website to a crawl, and the old platform was taken offline twice in one summer.
Partner guides and hotels could not see their own bookings, so they phoned the office to confirm each group.
Adventure Works wanted to sell packages that combine trips, activities and rooms in one basket, with prices that change with demand.
The scope was a booking platform that sells trips, activities and accommodation in one basket with live availability.
Deliverables were a booking service, an inventory service that holds live availability, a payment integration, a partner portal and a customer web and mobile front end.
Partners manage their own availability in the portal, and a change is visible to customers within seconds.
The platform supports package pricing and seasonal rules, which the commercial team maintains without developer help.
Accounting and the customer relationship system remained as they were and receive booking events from the platform.
Scope decisions were taken by the product manager with the commercial director, and anything that did not help the combined basket or the partner portal was moved to a later list.
Delivery took 12 months in four phases: foundation, trips, activities and accommodation, and the partner portal.
The team had 11 people, including five developers, two testers, a designer, a product manager and two operations specialists from Adventure Works.
The programme began in May 2023, the first trips were sold on the new platform in November 2023, and the partner portal opened in April 2024.
A load test at three times the previous peak was run before every release in the final three months.
Trips moved first because they were the biggest product line, and each later product followed after two weeks of stable running.
The platform runs on Azure with services deployed as containers on Kubernetes, and it scales out automatically during peak season.
Availability is held in Redis for fast reads and written to PostgreSQL, and a reservation is held for 15 minutes while the customer pays.
Payments go through a card payment provider that applies the strong customer authentication required by PSD2, and the platform never stores card numbers.
Events about each booking are published to Kafka for accounting and the customer relationship system, and the front end is built in React.
The partner portal signs users in with SAML or OAuth 2.0, and the booking API follows the OpenAPI 3.0 specification.
Online conversion rose from 2.1 percent to 3.4 percent of visits after the launch of the combined basket.
Rejected bookings after payment fell from 6 percent to under 1 percent.
The platform handled the summer peak of 2024, with 4 times the daily bookings of an average day, without an outage.
Holding a reservation for a short time while the customer paid removed most double sales, and the team recommends it for any shared inventory.
Partners asked for mobile access to the portal late in the project, so a mobile first design would have saved time.
The operations team now reviews booking and availability figures each Monday, and the platform dashboards were designed around the questions that review asks.
The commercial director chaired a fortnightly review where the product manager showed working software and the sales team gave feedback on the basket.

paragraphs: Wide World Importers order automation project.
Wide World Importers engaged us for its order automation project. Wide World Importers is a wholesale distributor of food and beverages that supplies restaurants and shops in Singapore.
Orders reached the sales desk by email, fax, phone and a customer web form, and clerks keyed each one into the order system, which took about 6 minutes for each order.
Keying errors affected 5 percent of orders, and each error led to a wrong delivery, a credit note or a phone call to the customer.
Customers could not see stock levels when they ordered, so substitutions were agreed by phone after the order was placed.
The sales desk worked until late every Thursday because restaurants placed their weekend orders at the last moment, and temporary staff were hired each month.
The scope was an order automation service that reads orders from email and the web form, matches them to products and customers, and creates the order without keying.
Deliverables were an email and document reader, a product matching service, a customer web portal with live stock, and an exceptions queue for the sales desk.
Orders that match with high confidence go straight through, and the rest wait in the queue with the suggested match shown for a clerk to confirm.
The portal shows stock levels and suggests substitutes when a product is not available, so the customer can decide at once.
The warehouse system and the finance system stayed the same, and the new service sends them orders through their existing interfaces.
The project did not change the way the warehouse picks or delivers goods, and the sales desk kept authority to override any order created by the service.
The project was delivered in 8 months in three phases: reading and matching, the exceptions queue, and the customer portal.
The team had 6 people, including a machine learning engineer, two developers, a tester, a business analyst and a delivery lead.
Work started in January 2024, the first customers went through the automatic flow in May 2024, and the portal launched in August 2024.
The matching service was trained on 18 months of past orders, and the sales desk reviewed its mistakes each week.
Phone orders were left for the last stage and are still taken by clerks, who now enter them in the portal.
A document reader extracts the lines from emails and attachments, and a Python service matches them to the product catalogue using text similarity.
Orders and the exceptions queue are stored in PostgreSQL, and a message queue on RabbitMQ decouples the reader from the order system.
The customer portal is built with Angular and calls a REST service, and customers sign in with accounts managed in Active Directory.
Orders are sent to the warehouse and finance systems as messages in the EDIFACT standard.
The share of orders created without keying rose to 82 percent within three months of launch.
Order errors fell from 5 percent to 1 percent, and credit notes for wrong deliveries fell by two thirds.
The sales desk no longer works late on Thursdays, and no temporary staff were hired in the year after launch.
Reviewing the matching mistakes every week built trust with the sales desk and improved accuracy faster than any change to the model.
Customers sent orders in many informal styles, so collecting real examples first was more useful than designing a clean input format.
The managing director followed progress through a one page report each month, which showed the share of orders handled automatically and the open exceptions.
The sales desk staff were involved from the first week, and two of the clerks became the owners of the exceptions queue after the launch.

paragraphs: Proseware billing modernisation project.
Proseware engaged us for its billing modernisation project. Proseware is a telecommunications provider that serves about 2 million mobile and broadband customers in Poland.
The billing system was 19 years old and ran on a platform whose vendor had announced the end of support.
A bill run took 31 hours, so errors found at the end meant waiting another day before bills could go out.
New tariffs needed code changes, which meant the marketing team waited about 4 months to launch an offer.
Customer service saw only a summary of the bill, so questions about charges were passed to a specialist team and took days to answer.
Regulators required itemised bills in a standard format, which the old system could produce only through a manual export.
The scope was a new billing platform that rates usage, applies tariffs and discounts, produces bills and feeds the ledger.
Deliverables were a rating engine, a tariff configuration tool for marketing, a bill generator, and a billing view for customer service.
The tariff tool lets marketing define plans, bundles and discounts without code changes, with a test mode that shows the effect on sample accounts.
Customer service sees every charge on a bill with an explanation, and can correct a charge with an approval step.
The network mediation system, which supplies the usage records, and the general ledger stayed as they were.
Security, audit and data protection requirements were agreed with the compliance team before design started, and each release was checked against them before it went to production.
Delivery took 20 months in five phases, beginning with prepaid products and ending with the largest postpaid segment.
The team had 22 people at its peak, including developers, testers, data migration specialists and business analysts, with a Proseware product owner.
The programme started in October 2022 and the last postpaid accounts were moved in May 2024.
Every phase ran a parallel bill run, in which old and new systems billed the same accounts and the differences were explained before the move.
Customer accounts were moved in waves of about 100,000, each followed by a week of close monitoring.
The rating engine runs on Java services on Kubernetes and processes usage records from a Kafka stream as they arrive.
Account and bill data is stored in Oracle with partitioning by month, and a copy is streamed to a reporting database.
Usage records follow the 3GPP charging data record format, and the itemised bill follows the format required by the regulator.
Payment files from banks are read in the ISO 20022 format, and postings go to the general ledger every night.
The bill run now takes 4 hours instead of 31, and bills go out on the planned day in every cycle.
Marketing launches a new offer in about 3 weeks instead of 4 months, without code changes.
Billing questions answered at the first contact rose from 38 percent to 77 percent.
The old billing platform was switched off after a final archive of its bills was checked, and the saved licence and hardware costs were reported separately to the finance team.
The parallel bill runs found 140 rules that nobody had written down, and the team treats them as the most valuable part of the programme.
Moving accounts in waves meant that a problem in one wave never reached more than a small part of the customer base.
The programme report to the board each quarter listed the number of accounts moved, the open differences from parallel runs and the risks that the steering group had accepted.
A steering group of finance, marketing, customer service and technology leaders met every month, and any difference found in a parallel run was reported to it.
